title: Regression harness orchestration and annotated trace collector runbook
content:
Purpose
This document describes a lightweight, reproducible orchestration pattern for perf CI runs that produce annotated traces (span+log bundles) and deterministic flamegraph artifacts suitable for automated regression detection and human triage. It is aimed at the serving runtime team: how to schedule jobs, inject realistic client behaviour, collect correlation-enabled traces, and store artifacts with stable names for downstream alerting and diffs.

Why this exists (context)
- We get intermittent tail regressions that are hard to correlate across commits because traces lack provenance and CI jobs are noisy.
- Existing samplers and flamegraph collectors are powerful but inconsistent about job lifecycle and artifact naming.
- Goal: make perf CI a single-click reproducible run that yields: latency histograms, per-request annotated traces (request id -> trace bundle), top-down flamegraphs for CPU and allocation, and a short triage checklist.

Design overview
- Orchestration model: a controller (k8s CronJob or GitHub Actions workflow) that: (1) deploys a short-lived load-generator pod, (2) applies warmup policy to K/V cache and KV state, (3) runs the steady-state workload, (4) triggers collectors (eBPF & runtime agent), (5) collects and uploads artifacts to an artifact bucket with stable prefixes.
- Trace annotation: every synthetic client request attaches a correlation header X-RDWD-RunId and X-RDWD-ReqId. The load-generator ensures those headers are propagated. Collectors enrich traces with these headers so a single request can be mapped to spans, logs, and token-level events.
- Artifact schema (S3 / GCS prefix): /perf-ci/{branch}/{build}/{run_ts}/{model}/{scenario}/
  - latency.csv (P50,P90,P95,P99 distributions)
  - traces/{reqid}-{spanroot}.har (protobuf/zip of spans + logs)
  - flamegraphs/cpu-{threadgroup}.svg
  - flamegraphs/alloc-{threadgroup}.svg
  - env.json (scrubbed runtime config, commit sha, node labels)

Orchestration templates (high-level)
- GitHub Actions: short-lived runner job that checks out runtime binary, launches a k8s job via kubectl apply, waits for completion, grabs artifacts via gsutil, uploads to GH artifacts or to perf-bucket and posts summary. Use action matrix to run across 2-3 model sizes in parallel.
- k8s CronJob: for nightly regression baseline; includes strong tainting so can land on perf nodes. Use TTL controller to prune old jobs.

Warmup & workload details
- Warmup policy: prefix-kvcache-fill -> read-mix for 2x expected token cache window; ensures realistic KV cache hit rate. Warmup script emits warmup.done sentinel to the controller.
- Workload mix: schedule a mixed distribution of small-chat (short seq) and long-generation (long seq) requests with configurable ratios. Use synthetic randomness seed logged into env.json so runs are reproducible.
- Client jitter injection: add controlled inter-request jitter +/- 10ms to avoid pathological batching. Use header X-RDWD-Seed for seed.

Collectors and instrumentation
- Runtime agent (userland): lightweight HTTP endpoint that can be told to start/stop collecting callstacks and to dump in folded format. Use agent to capture KV cache metrics at second granularity.
- eBPF probe: limited to stack sampling + syscall counts (avoid heavy sampling). Default sampling rate 200Hz for 20s windows to produce flamegraphs.
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry trace exporter that writes to a local file sink (OTLP->file) during CI to avoid external dependencies; file then uploaded with artifacts. Ensure traces include attributes: run_id, req_id, model_name, model_version, node_id, and batch_size.

Collector invocation sequence
1. Wait for workload steady-state (observed P50 within target +- 5% for 30s).
2. Start runtime agent snapshot mode and eBPF sampler simultaneously. Start timer for sample window (configurable, default 20s).
3. Tag the window in logs with RUN_WINDOW_START/RUN_WINDOW_END and the run_id.
4. When done, signal collectors to flush. Collectors write to /tmp/artifacts in pod.
5. Copy artifacts from pods (kubectl cp) and upload.

Naming and provenance policy
- run_id: {branch}-{short-sha}-{utc-YYYYMMDDTHHMMSS} e.g., main-3b7f2c-20241205T023045
- req_id: uuidv4 prefixed with run_id.
- env.json must contain: commit_sha, build_number (if available), run_id, cluster_name, node_labels, generator_seed, scenario_name.

Alerting and regression detection hooks
- A separate lightweight job parses last N runs for the same branch+scenario and computes deltas for P99 and tail mass. If P99 increases by > 15% or tail mass > threshold, fail CI and create JIRA ticket template with links to artifacts.
- When failing, include the minimal repro: the first req_id that exceeded threshold, the env.json for that run, and the associated full trace bundle. This makes human triage immediate.

Triage checklist (quick)
- Check env.json: model version or quantization changes?
- Compare warmup.done timestamp vs run start: insufficient warmup often causes higher tail.
- Open traces/{reqid} to examine span durations: look for blocking syscalls or GC pauses.
- For flamegraphs: compare last-good vs current via diffoscope (or `flamegraph.pl --compare`). Focus on hot callsites with large delta at the P99 path.
- Node-level metrics: CPU steal, RTX memory alloc stalls (see node labels).

Common failure modes and mitigations
- Excessive tail after upgrade to new allocator: reproduce locally with same seed and extended profiling window (60s). If stable, roll back allocator flags or add backpressure knobs.
- Skewed KV cache: if hit rate < expected, replay warmup with larger prefix, or inspect cached keys frequency in traces.
- Noisy eBPF signals: reduce sample frequency or sample a subset of threads using threadgroup filter.

Operational runbook (step-by-step)
1. Kick off the GH Actions job via comment / rerun or trigger nightly CronJob.
2. Monitor job logs in GH/k8s. Wait for warmup.done.
3. After collectors finish, download artifacts to local machine or perf-bucket.
4. Run local sanity script: scripts/perfci/check-artefacts.sh which validates env.json, ensures at least 1000 requests recorded and P90 within nominal range.
5. If failure: gather first-bad-req-id, download traces and flamegraphs, and open triage ticket using template. Attach env.json and short-run summary.

Lightweight helper scripts (descriptions)
- generator/warmup.py: seeds KV cache with a reproducible pattern and emits warmup.done
- collector/agent-control.sh: start | stop | dump folded stacks | upload
- tooling/metric-compare.py: compare metrics from two runs and produce CSV delta

Example snippet: run_id generation (shell)
- RUN_ID=$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)

Best practices / notes
- Keep sampling windows short and repeat runs to account for noise. Prefer median-of-5 for P99 signal when triaging.
- Scrub secrets from env.json before upload. Use role-based write-only service account for artifact bucket.
- Prefer deterministic seeds for synthetic traffic. Randomness is fine for nightly baselines but CI regression checks should be seeded.

Open questions / followups
- Integrate with the new centralized tracing backend without blowing up cost: can we sample only request ids that exceed latency thresholds?
- Can we automate trace-to-flamegraph mapping so that the exact stack for the slow request is highlighted in the flamegraph UI?

Appendix: Links to helper PRs and tickets
- PR: runtime: add agent dump endpoint -> https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/842
- JIRA: RT-3782 Perf CI baseline alerts

Notes to self (todo)
- add Kubernetes job templates for ARM nodes and CPU-only runs
- add more robust pruning for old artifacts (TTL 90d)
- follow up with SRE on perf node taints and node selector naming

-- end of runbook --
